etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pase, from Anglo-Norman pas, Old French pas, and their source, Latin passus. Doublet of pas and fathom; compare also pass. Cognate with Spanish pasear.

definitions.definition: A step taken with the foot. [from 14th c.]
The distance covered in a step (or sometimes two), either vaguely or according to various specific set measurements.[1] [from 14th c.]
A manner of walking, running or dancing; the rate or style of how someone moves with their feet. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 2012 June 9, Owen Phillips, “Euro 2012: Netherlands 0-1 Denmark”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: Netherlands, one of the pre-tournament favourites, combined their undoubted guile, creativity, pace and attacking quality with midfield grit and organisation.

definitions.definition: Any of various gaits of a horse, specifically a 2-beat, lateral gait. [from 15th c.]
Speed or velocity in general. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto IX”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 14, page 311:
quote.text: For with ſuch puiſſance and impetuous maine / Thoſe Champions broke on them, that forſt the fly, / Like ſcattered Sheepe, whenas the Shepherds ſwaine / A Lyon and a Tigre doth eſpye, / With greedy pace forth ruſhing from the foreſt nye.

quote.citation: 1983, Kathryn Lance, Running for Health, Bantam, →ISBN:
quote.text: The fastest women runners can run a mile in well under five minutes, but in order to reach that goal they've had to train at a much slower pace over thousands of miles.

definitions.definition: (cricket) A measure of the hardness of a pitch and of the tendency of a cricket ball to maintain its speed after bouncing. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 1952, G. B. Stern, The Donkey Shoe, The Macmillan Company, published 1952, page 29:
quote.text: […]  but at Broadstairs and other places along the coast, a pace of donkeys stood on the sea-shore expectant (at least, their owners were expectant) of children clamouring to ride.

quote.citation: 2006 November 9, “Drop the dead donkeys”, in The Economist:
quote.text: A pace of donkeys fans out in different directions.

quote.citation: 2007, Elinor De Wire, The Lightkeepers' Menagerie: Stories of Animals at Lighthouses, Pineapple Press, published 2007, →ISBN, page 200:
quote.text: Like a small farm, the lighthouse compound had its chattering of chicks, pace of donkeys, troop of horses, and fold of sheep.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A passage through difficult terrain; a mountain pass or route vulnerable to ambush etc. [14th–17th c.]

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: But when she saw them gone she forward went, / As lay her journey, through that perlous Pace [...].

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An aisle in a church. [15th–19th c.]
(cricket) Describing a bowler who bowls fast balls.
To walk back and forth in a small distance.

quote.citation: 1874, Marcus Clarke, For the Term of His Natural Life, Chapter V:
quote.text: Groups of men, in all imaginable attitudes, were lying, standing, sitting, or pacing up and down.

definitions.definition: To set the speed in a race. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin pāce (“in peace”), ablative form of pāx (“peace”).

quote.citation: 1998, Harold Bloom, Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human:
quote.text: She is marvelous here, but he (pace many critics) is no bumpkin
